item.title: Initial Field Test of a Quadrupedal Robot at SLAC Beam Dump East (BDE): A Sandbox for Robotics in Accelerator Operations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deploying field robotics in large scale particle accelerator facilities offers significant potential to enhance operational efficiency, promote facility sustainability, and reduce personnel exposure to radiation and other hazards. As key underlying technologies mature, field robotics are seeing broader deployment across various industrial sectors. However, accelerator facilities have remained cautious in adopting these systems, primarily due to concerns regarding cost versus return on investment and the risk of equipment collisions. In addition, operational experience with SLAC's Remotely Operated Accelerator Monitoring platform, ROAM highlighted critical technical challenges, including radiation tolerance and poor network connectivity in enclosed accelerator areas. This paper presents the findings from a recent test drive of a Boston Dynamics SPOT quadrupedal robot equipped with a SPOT Arm payload conducted at SLAC's Beam Dump East facility. We evaluate the technical feasibility and operational considerations of deploying quadrupedal field robotics within accelerator environments. Furthermore, we report key practical challenges, such as protective suits that impede navigation sensors and low light infrared navigation in unlit spaces. Finally, we outline potential development pathways toward adaptive learning and autonomous execution for future routine field robotics operations in accelerator facilities.
item.dc:creator: M. Bai (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), M. A. Montironi (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), A. Saad (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), T. Thayer (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory)

item.title: Optimization of Piezo Operation for Superconducting TESLA Cavities at EuXFEL
item.description: arXiv:2611.31086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting cavities with high-Q factor require precise tuning to match the RF frequency, ensuring stable electromagnetic fields and minimizing RF power consumption. At the European XFEL (EuXFEL) accelerator, TESLA cavities are tuned using slow tuners (step motors) for coarse adjustments and fast tuners (piezoelectric actuators) for fine-tuning and compensating disturbances such as Lorentz Force Detuning (LFD). Piezo actuators, critical to this system, require high-voltage (up to 100V) and high-current (up to 1A) driving signals for effective LFD compensation. However, they are vulnerable to overvoltage, overcurrent, and overheating, and their protection is crucial since replacing damaged piezos in fully assembled modules is infeasible. Additionally, piezo-induced vibrations can affect the machine's stability. Optimizing piezo excitation, by reducing voltage, current, and current slope while ensuring effective LFD compensation, improves equally efficiency, reliability and machine stability. This paper explores the optimization of piezo excitation at EuXFEL, detailing methods and results applicable to other facilities with superconducting cavities as well.

item.title: Towards Automatic Ion Identification in Storage Rings
item.description: arXiv:2611.28070v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Resonant Schottky detectors provide non-destructive, single-ion-sensitive measurements of revolution frequencies and intensities of ion species stored in a heavy-ion storage ring. These high-\(Q\) cavities allow analysis of high-order harmonics of the revolution frequencies to magnify absolute frequency separations. Adjacent harmonic ranges can, however, overlap within the detector band, making frequency alone insufficient for determining the ion's mass-to-charge ratio $(m/q)$. We present a proof-of-concept for an automated harmonic de-overlapping method using spectral shapes in combined Schottky and Isochronous Mass Spectrometry. The empirical ansatz is that, for a fixed ion-optical setting, each peak, corresponding to a specific ion species with given $m/q$ ratio, has a characteristic profile that evolves smoothly with changing $m/q$. Occurrences of the same local structure at different harmonics should therefore retain almost identical shapes after frequency rescaling. Applied to a 245\,MHz spectrum accumulated from 11\,452 injections at the Experimental Storage Ring at GSI, the method organizes 16 of 32 detected structures into five candidate families and reconstructs their fundamental-frequency representation. Reducing the complex mixed-harmonic spectrum to this smaller candidate set solves the challenging task of finding initial anchors for the ion identification.
item.dc:creator: Anna Jule He{\ss}, David Freire-Fern\'andez, Moritz Porstend\"orfer, Wolfram Korten, Yury A. Litvinov

item.title: A muonium laser ionization system for muon acceleration studies at J-PARC
item.description: arXiv:2611.30375v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper reports the development and commissioning of a muonium ionization laser system installed in the H2 area of the J-PARC Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility for muon accelerator studies. In this accelerator scheme, ultraslow muons generated by laser ionization of thermal muonium atoms serve as the particle source for subsequent radio-frequency acceleration. The laser system generates coherent 122-nm pulses for muonium excitation and 355-nm pulses for photoionization of the excited muonium. A vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) pulse transport system and VUV pulse diagnostics were also developed. Muonium ionization was confirmed using a 5.7~keV muon transport line, and a muon rate of approximately 6~s$^{-1}$ was observed. These results establish operation of the ionization system and provide a platform for subsequent muon accelerator studies.
item.dc:creator: Shusei Kamioka, Meng Lyu, Katsuyoshi Homma, Tsutomu Mibe, Shinki Nakamura, Yu Oishi, Koichiro Shimomura, Tatsuya Shinozaki, Hikaru Sunagawa, Satoshi Wada, Takumi Yamada, Takayuki Yamazaki

item.title: Transverse deflecting cavities
item.description: arXiv:1201.2600v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transverse deflecting cavities are used for a number of applications in modern accelerators. In this paper we discuss the fields of these cavities, some of their applications, and some important aspects of their design.
item.dc:creator: G. Burt (Lancaster University)

item.title: An Innovative Photon-Driven Subcritical Reactor Concept Powered by Synchrotron Radiation Source
item.description: arXiv:2509.01249v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most reactors are fuelled with enriched uranium, whose production is proliferation-sensitive and concentrated in a few suppliers, and discharge fuel that still contains fissile material and accumulates in storage. Accelerator-driven subcritical reactors relax the requirements on the fuel, but proton beams must travel in vacuum to a spallation target inside the core. Here we show that synchrotron radiation can drive a subcritical heavy-water reactor fuelled with natural uranium or with spent fuel loaded without reprocessing. A photon beam with a critical energy of 10 MeV, from a proposed 32 GeV electron storage ring, releases neutrons in a uranium converter at the centre of the core. Coupled photon-neutron Monte Carlo simulations show that the two cores, loading different fuels but being at a multiplication factor close to 0.985, reach the same gain: one 400 kW beamline drives each of them close to 4.4 MW of fission power, about 11 times the beam power. A storage ring with 50 beamlines could drive one core from each beamline, every core controlled through its own photon beam. These results make synchrotron radiation a candidate driver for thermal subcritical reactors that need neither enrichment nor reprocessing, complementary to proton-driven fast systems for transmutation.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Cammi, Lorenzo Loi, Andrea Missaglia, David Alesini, Hans-Heinrich Braun

item.title: Exact 1D Nonlinear Solutions for Proton-Driven Plasma Wakefields
item.description: arXiv:2607.06458v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The analytical modeling of a plasma wakefield driven by a relativistic proton beam is an element in optimizing advanced plasma-based acceleration schemes. In this work, we present a 1D nonlinear fluid framework under the quasi-static approximation to describe the wake potential excited by a positively charged proton driver which attracts background electrons into a density compression rather than expelling them. We extend the classical 1D nonlinear relativistic plasma wakefield paradigm to evaluate the fluid profiles driven by intense relativistic proton trains under the comoving coordinate approximation. Using a two-bunch scheme, our piecewise-event integration model is validated to high numerical accuracy ($\sim 10^{-11}~\mathrm{GV/m}$) against independent phase-space quadrature of cold-fluid solutions, confirming that interface boundary corners represent physical step discontinuities in the second potential derivative. Scaling to an $N=100$ ramped micro-bunch train with fixed $2\pi$ spacing, we resolve macroscopic phase-accumulation and subsequent nonlinear detuning by deriving a piecewise analytical scaling model. This formulation maps the initial unattenuated quadratic coherent growth alongside the flat asymptotic post-train residual wake plateau, which is determined exactly by the conserved vacuum Hamiltonian invariant evaluated at the final bunch-train exit state. Furthermore, the framework estimates the onset of nonlinear phase-slippage that arrests growth and causes the transient wakefield overshoot to decay toward the residual horizon. Providing immediate 1D analytical benchmarks, this computationally inexpensive tool offers a reproducible baseline for verifying 1D fluid and multi-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) codes. It also provides a tractable starting point for exploring asymmetric, custom-shaped driver profiles relevant to transformer-ratio optimization.
item.dc:creator: D. Tsiklauri
